notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize the money robbed from houses arranged in a circle, with no two adjacent houses chosen. The input contains at least one house.
Idea: Handle the one-house case directly; otherwise solve two linear robber problems, excluding the last house in one and the first house in the other.
Technique and why it applies: Excluding one endpoint breaks the circular conflict, leaving the standard non-adjacent dynamic program. helper keeps two rolling best totals and chooses between robbing the current house and skipping it.
Invariant: During helper, one and two represent the best totals for the two preceding prefixes; its return is the best amount for that linear slice.
Edge cases: A single house returns its value. For two or more houses, every valid circular selection omits at least one of the two endpoints, so one of the two helper calls covers it.
Complexity: Each helper is linear, so time is O(n). The nums slices create O(n) temporary lists, so auxiliary space is O(n), not O(1). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum non-adjacent house sum when the first and last houses are neighbors in a circle.
Idea: Compare the best result from robbing the range that excludes the last house with the best result from the range that excludes the first.
Technique and why it applies: robRange performs linear dynamic programming with rolling values; splitting the circle into these two ranges prevents selecting both circularly adjacent endpoints.
Invariant: Within robRange, num_i is the best total through the current house, while num_i_1 and num_i_2 hold the prior states used for the recurrence.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero, although the statement guarantees at least one house; one house returns nums[0]. For two houses, the two ranges each contain one eligible house.
Complexity: The two range scans together take O(n) time. Only a constant number of rolling variables are used, and the method does not create sliced arrays, so O(1) auxiliary space is accurate.

Task and constraints: Produce the shortest palindrome by adding characters only to the front of s; the string may be empty and contains lowercase letters.
Idea: Find the longest prefix that is already a palindrome, then reverse the remaining suffix and prepend it.
Technique and why it applies: The loop tests each prefix s[:i] against its reverse and remembers the largest matching length through end. Any suffix after that prefix must be mirrored in front to make the whole string a palindrome.
Invariant: After each tested i, end records the final index of the longest palindromic prefix seen so far.
Edge cases: An already-palindromic string returns immediately. For an empty string, the first check succeeds and returns it. For a string with no longer palindromic prefix, the first character still forms a one-character palindrome.
Complexity: The loop repeatedly creates and reverses prefixes, leading to O(n²) time and O(n) temporary/output space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Add the fewest characters to the front of s to make it a palindrome; empty input is permitted.
Idea: Build a prefix-function table over s followed by its reverse, then use the table to locate a suitable palindromic prefix length.
Technique and why it applies: getPrefix is a KMP-style border computation that reuses prior matches instead of comparing every prefix independently. The loop backs off while the matched length is at least len(s), then the remaining suffix is reversed and prepended.
Invariant: prefix[i] stores the length-minus-one index of the longest proper border for the processed pattern prefix; the fallback follows these border links.
Edge cases: Empty s returns immediately. The concatenation is formed without a separator, so repeated content across the boundary can affect prefix matches; the extra fallback loop is intended to restrict the match to a valid prefix length.
Complexity: Prefix construction and fallback are O(n) time; the concatenated string and prefix list use O(n) space. The author labels are consistent with these bounds.

Task and constraints: Construct the shortest palindrome by prepending characters to a string of lowercase letters, including the empty string.
Idea: Transform the string with separators, run Manacher's palindrome-radius algorithm, and retain the longest palindrome whose left boundary reaches the start.
Technique and why it applies: The center/right pair reuses previously computed palindrome radii; mirrored radii provide a lower bound before expansion. The final slice reverses the suffix beyond the longest palindromic prefix.
Invariant: palindrome[i] stores the radius around transformed-string position i; center and right identify the palindrome reaching farthest to the right among processed centers.
Edge cases: preProcess handles an empty string with sentinels. The code overwrites max_len for each qualifying center, so it relies on the scan order to leave the longest qualifying prefix at the end.
Complexity: Transformation, radius computation, and final scan are O(n) time and O(n) space. The supplied labels are correct for the implementation.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest palindrome obtainable by adding characters at the front, with input length up to 50,000.
Idea: Use a KMP prefix-function on s + '#' + reverse(s), then prepend the reversed suffix beyond the longest prefix match.
Technique and why it applies: The separator prevents a border from matching through the boundary between s and its reverse. getPrefix computes border lengths in linear time; its final entry gives the longest palindromic prefix length.
Invariant: At each index, prefix stores the longest proper prefix matching a suffix of the processed pattern, with fallback links reused after mismatches.
Edge cases: Empty input returns unchanged before indexing prefix[-1]. The separator is safe because the input is restricted to lowercase English letters.
Complexity: Building the concatenation and prefix table takes O(n) time and O(n) space, followed by a linear slice/reversal. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the kth largest array element by sorted position, counting duplicate values separately. The prompt asks for O(n) time.
Idea: Sort the entire array in descending order and return the element at index k-1.
Technique and why it applies: Descending sort places the largest value first, so the kth position directly gives the requested answer.
Invariant: After sorting, nums[i] is the element at rank i+1 in descending order.
Edge cases: k=1 returns the maximum; k=len(nums) returns the minimum. Duplicate values remain in the sorted list and count toward rank, as required.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n) time in typical comparison-sort analysis, so this code does not satisfy the required O(n) time target. It sorts in place, with Python's sort using implementation-dependent temporary memory; no author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Select the kth largest value without needing to sort the full array; duplicates count as separate positions.
Idea: Repeatedly partition around a random pivot, placing values larger than the pivot to its left, and narrow the search interval to the target index k-1.
Technique and why it applies: Quickselect only continues in the partition containing the desired rank. PartitionAroundPivot mutates nums in place and returns the pivot's final descending-order position.
Invariant: After partitioning, every value to the left of the pivot is greater than it and every value to the right is less than or equal to it; the target rank is sought in the relevant side.
Edge cases: k=1 seeks the maximum and k=len(nums) seeks the minimum. Random pivots reduce expected bad partitions, but do not guarantee linear worst-case time.
Complexity: Expected time is O(n), worst case O(n²); auxiliary space is O(1) aside from recursion-free local state. The author label correctly states average linear time and constant space.

Task and constraints: Return the kth largest value, with duplicates counted, from an unsorted array.
Idea: Use randomized three-way quickselect so that equal pivot values occupy a middle partition, then read nums[k-1].
Technique and why it applies: tri_partition separates values according to the comparator and returns the equal-value interval. The algorithm narrows left/right to the side containing the requested descending rank; three-way partitioning handles duplicate-heavy inputs efficiently.
Invariant: Values before the equal partition rank ahead of it under the chosen descending comparator; values in the equal partition share the pivot value.
Edge cases: Valid k is guaranteed. If k-1 lies within the equal partition, selection stops without further partitioning.
Complexity: Randomized selection is expected O(n) time but can be O(n²) in the worst case. The algorithm mutates nums and uses O(1) auxiliary space. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return whether any integer appears at least twice in nums.
Idea: Convert nums to a set and compare the number of unique values with the original length.
Technique and why it applies: A set removes duplicate occurrences, so its size is smaller exactly when at least one duplicate exists.
Invariant: set(nums) contains one representative of every distinct value in nums; the two lengths therefore encode whether duplicates were present.
Edge cases: A one-element list returns False. Multiple copies of any value make the lengths differ, including when every item is identical.
Complexity: Constructing the set takes O(n) expected time and O(n) additional space for n elements. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the array contains any repeated value.
Idea: Compare the original list length with the length of a set constructed from it.
Technique and why it applies: Set conversion retains only distinct values. A shorter set proves at least one original occurrence was duplicated.
Invariant: The set contains exactly the distinct elements seen in nums; its size equals nums length if and only if all values are distinct.
Edge cases: An array with no repeats returns False; any repeated value returns True. The expression returns a Boolean directly.
Complexity: Set construction and length comparison take O(n) expected time and O(n) space. The author-provided O(n) time and space labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Produce sorted skyline key points for rectangles described by left edge, right edge, and height. Adjacent horizontal segments of equal height must be merged.
Idea: Group building start and end events by x-coordinate, maintain active heights, and emit a point when the active maximum changes.
Technique and why it applies: Positive events add a building height; negative events remove that height. active is kept sorted ascending so active[-1] represents the current maximum.
Invariant: After processing each event at x, active should contain the heights of all buildings covering the interval immediately to the right of x, and result records changes in the maximum.
Edge cases: Simultaneous events are sorted so starts are handled before ends at each x. The shown snippet does not import collections or bisect_left, so it raises NameError unless those names are provided elsewhere. Insert/index operations on active are linear.
Complexity: Sorting events is O(n log n), but repeated active.insert and active.index can make event processing O(n²); storage is O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return True if equal values occur at two distinct indices whose distance is at most k; otherwise return False.
Idea: Scan left to right and remember the most recent index for each value.
Technique and why it applies: If a value has been seen before, the current index minus its stored latest index is the smallest possible distance to a prior equal value. A qualifying distance returns immediately.
Invariant: After each iteration, seen maps each processed value to its latest index, allowing the next occurrence to be checked against the nearest previous one.
Edge cases: k=0 always returns False because distinct indices cannot have distance zero. A duplicate farther than k updates the remembered index so later occurrences are compared to the closest previous one.
Complexity: The single pass takes O(n) expected time and the dictionary uses O(n) space. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check for equal values at distinct indices no more than k apart.
Idea: Store the latest index for each value, test the gap on repeats, and update the index when the prior occurrence is too far away.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing against the latest occurrence is sufficient because it minimizes the index distance among all earlier matches.
Invariant: lookup contains the most recent processed index for each value; any repeated value is tested against that closest prior position.
Edge cases: k=0 returns False for every valid input. For a value repeated with a gap greater than k, the stored index is refreshed, allowing a later close duplicate to be detected.
Complexity: The array is scanned once, with O(n) expected time and O(n) space. The author labels are consistent.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two values differ by at most t and their indices differ by at most k.
Idea: Maintain a sliding OrderedDict window and bucket values so only the same or neighboring buckets need comparison.
Technique and why it applies: For t>0, integer division groups nearby values; candidate values from bucket-1, bucket, and bucket+1 are checked with the exact absolute-difference condition. The oldest entry is removed when the window exceeds k.
Invariant: Before testing the current number, window contains values from the preceding k positions at most, keyed by their buckets.
Edge cases: Negative k or t returns False. When t=0, each number itself is used as its bucket, so only exact duplicates match. Each bucket stores one value, relying on values sharing a bucket being within the threshold.
Complexity: Each iteration checks three buckets and updates the ordered map, giving O(n) expected time and O(k) window space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the area of the largest all-'1' square in a nonempty binary matrix.
Idea: Use dynamic programming where each cell stores the side length of the largest all-one square ending at that cell.
Technique and why it applies: For a '1', the side is one plus the minimum of the top, left, and top-left DP values. Any zero among those neighboring structures limits the square size.
Invariant: dp[i][j] is the maximal square side ending at (i,j); result tracks the largest side encountered.
Edge cases: Border cells use zero for missing neighbors. If the matrix contains no '1', result remains zero and the returned area is zero.
Complexity: Every cell is visited once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) space for the DP matrix. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the area of the largest square containing only ones in a binary matrix.
Idea: Fill a DP table of square side lengths using the minimum of the top, left, and diagonal states.
Technique and why it applies: For a cell containing '1', the three neighboring square sizes constrain how large a square can end there; adding one extends their shared square. Zero cells keep size zero.
Invariant: size[i][j] is the side length of the largest all-one square ending at cell (i,j), and max_size is the largest side observed.
Edge cases: The empty-matrix guard returns zero. The implementation initializes max_size from the first row but does not update it when a later row's first-column cell is '1'; a matrix such as [['0'],['1']] therefore incorrectly returns zero.
Complexity: The table has m*n cells, so time and space are O(mn). The author labels O(n²) assume a square matrix; for general m-by-n inputs the precise bound is O(mn).

Task and constraints: Return the area of the largest all-one square, with an explicit empty-matrix check.
Idea: First calculate consecutive vertical and horizontal run lengths from each cell, then use a second DP table to determine square sizes.
Technique and why it applies: table[i][j] stores downward height and rightward width of the one-run. The second pass limits each square by those runs and by the diagonal neighbor's square size plus one.
Invariant: At each cell, side cannot exceed its local horizontal/vertical runs or one plus the square available diagonally below-right.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. The code checks the diagonal row width before reading s[i+1][j+1], supporting rectangular matrices. The first table uses O(mn) entries and the second another O(mn).
Complexity: Both passes are O(mn) time and O(mn) space. The author labels O(n²) describe square matrices; for arbitrary dimensions, O(mn) is more precise.

Task and constraints: Compute the area of the largest square made entirely of ones.
Idea: Apply the standard square-side recurrence but retain only the previous and current DP rows.
Technique and why it applies: For each '1', the side length is one plus the minimum of its left neighbor in the current row, its upper neighbor, and its upper-left neighbor. A '0' resets the state to zero.
Invariant: size[i % 2][j] represents the current row's square size, while size[(i-1) % 2] retains the previous row.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. max_size is updated across the first row and inner columns, but not when a later row's first-column cell is '1'; for example [['0'],['1']] incorrectly returns zero.
Complexity: Each cell is processed once, so time is O(mn); the two DP rows use O(n) auxiliary space. The author labels O(n²) time and O(n) space are only accurate for time if the matrix is square; generally time is O(mn).

Task and constraints: Return the combined area of two axis-aligned rectangles, subtracting their overlap so it is not counted twice.
Idea: Compute both individual areas and subtract the area of their intersection.
Technique and why it applies: segment calculates positive overlap length for one axis using the smaller upper endpoint minus the larger lower endpoint; if the intervals do not overlap with positive length, it returns zero. Multiplying horizontal and vertical overlap gives intersection area.
Invariant: The result equals area(A)+area(B)-area(A∩B), so every covered point is counted once.
Edge cases: Identical rectangles subtract one full area, leaving that area. Rectangles touching only along an edge or at a point have zero overlap area.
Complexity: A fixed number of min/max operations gives O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.
